title: Boss warm-up: draft the replies
brief: A team wants an assistant that drafts replies to customer emails. They have not said how many, how risky or how fast. Practise all five moves in three minutes, aloud.

blocks.text: Warm up before the real boss levels

steps.title: Clarify
steps.md: Three or four questions about volume, risk, data needs and review.

steps.title: Options
steps.md: Name three or four, including the boring one.

steps.title: Pick and flip
steps.md: Choose for assumed dials and say what flips it.

steps.title: Failure modes
steps.md: Two failures, each with a detection signal.

steps.title: Metrics and rollout
steps.md: Two metrics and a staged rollout.

blocks.title: How to use this level
blocks.md: Set a timer for three minutes and answer aloud before you open the model answer. Then score yourself with the rubric. The goal is the shape, not a perfect design.

quiz.q: Which opening is strongest for this question?
options: I would fine-tune a model on our past replies so it learns the company voice and policy
I would build RAG with a vector database over every past email in the archive
I would first ask about volume, tone rules, approval and the cost of a wrong reply
I would use the largest available model at temperature 0 and send the drafts directly
quiz.explain: The strongest answers ask for dials before naming a technology. Fine-tuning is weak for facts, a vector database may be unnecessary, and the largest model at temperature 0 sends outbound text with no review or risk analysis.

quiz.q: Select every item that belongs in step 5, metrics and rollout.
options: Share of drafts that humans send with no edits
Policy violations caught per thousand drafts
A staged rollout: shadow mode, then a small canary
The list of options you considered
The dials you asked about at the start
quiz.explain: Edit rate and violation rate are metrics, and a staged rollout is the rollout plan. The options belong in step 2 and the dials belong in step 1.

quiz.q: You proposed human-reviewed drafts. The team asks to auto-send replies for one low-risk category. Which dial moved, and what changes?
options: Risk fell for one category, so auto-send there with monitoring
Risk is irrelevant to the design, so remove review for every category
Volume moved, so switch to fine-tuning for every reply category
Latency moved, so remove evaluation because the reviewers are gone
quiz.explain: The risk dial moved for one category, so the flip is narrow: auto-send there with monitoring and a rollback switch, and keep review for the rest. Removing review everywhere ignores risk, and the other options change dials that did not move.

defend.prompt: A team wants an assistant that drafts replies to customer emails. How would you approach it?
clarify: How many emails arrive per day, and how fast must a draft appear?
Who reviews drafts before sending, and what does a wrong reply cost?
What data do replies need: policy documents, past replies or live account data?
Which tone and compliance rules apply, and is any customer data restricted?
Which languages and channels are in scope?

options.name: Prompt with templates and style rules
options.when: A small set of reply types and stable policies.
options.tradeoff: Cheap and simple, but policies drift and long prompts raise cost per draft.

options.name: RAG over policies and past replies
options.when: A large or changing policy set where citations help reviewers.
options.tradeoff: Retrieval quality becomes the ceiling, and it adds moving parts.

options.name: Tools for account and order lookups
options.when: Replies need live data from a system of record.
options.tradeoff: Tool permissions and extra latency need care.

options.name: Fine-tuning for tone
options.when: A consistent voice is needed at high volume, or a smaller model is wanted.
options.tradeoff: Weak for facts, so it does not replace retrieval.

modelAnswer.md: **1. Clarify the dials.** I would ask how many emails arrive and how fast a draft must appear, who reviews drafts and what a wrong reply costs, what data a reply needs, and which tone and compliance rules apply.

**2. List the options, including the boring one.** The boring option is a prompt with templates and style rules. The alternatives are RAG over policies and past replies, tools for live account lookups, fine-tuning for tone and human approval before sending.

**3. Pick for the stated dials, and say what flips it.** With no more detail I would assume moderate volume, a policy set that changes monthly, per-customer data and a human reviewer. I would start with a prompt plus RAG over the policies, a lookup tool for order data and human approval. If one reply category is low risk I would allow auto-send there. If the policy set is tiny and stable I would drop RAG and use a cached prompt. If volume grows a lot I would add routing and caching.

**4. Name failure modes and how I would detect them.** A draft invents a policy, which I would catch with a groundedness check and a golden set of real emails. A draft leaks another customer's data, which I would catch with access checks on every lookup and a leakage test set.

**5. Name metrics and the rollout.** I would track the share of drafts sent with no edits, policy violations per thousand drafts, p95 time to a draft and cost per draft. I would run in shadow mode first, then a small canary, with a switch to roll back.

rubric.pt: Asks about volume, risk, data needs and review before naming a technology
Names at least three options, including the boring one
Picks for stated or assumed dials instead of a favourite tool
States at least one explicit flip condition with a dial and a threshold
Names failure modes with a detection signal
Names metrics and a staged rollout

followUps.q: The team wants to auto-send password-reset replies. What changes?
followUps.a: The risk dial is low for that category, so allow auto-send only there with groundedness and policy checks and a rollback switch. Keep review elsewhere and watch the edit rate and complaint rate.

followUps.q: Volume grows tenfold. What breaks first?
followUps.a: Latency and cost per draft, and retrieval load. Flip toward routing, prompt caching and batch processing for non-urgent replies, which worlds 1, 2 and 16 cover.

followUps.q: How would you test the assistant before launch?
followUps.a: Build a golden set of real emails with approved replies, judge drafts with a rubric plus human spot checks, and compare in shadow mode before any customer sees a draft. World 14 covers evaluation.

redFlags: Names a vector database or a model before asking any question
Treats fine-tuning as the way to add policy knowledge
Ignores risk and review for outbound customer messages
Ends without metrics or a rollout plan

takeaways: Practise the five moves aloud against a timebox until the shape is automatic
Assume dials when you cannot ask, and say that you are assuming
A good flip names one dial and one threshold
Close with metrics and a staged rollout, not with a tool name
